topic.title: 'No added sugar' is a font size
topic.claim: Most 'healthy' snack packs moved the bad stuff from the front of the pack to the back, and charged more for the move.
topic.moment: You pick the granola that says 'no refined sugar' in green and pay double.

turn.actually: The claim is on the front; the dates, honey and oil are in the small print.

topic.feeling: I paid to feel good, not to eat better.
topic.villain: Front-of-pack labels that are marketing, not information
topic.because: A health word lets a brand charge more for the same calories. Few people turn the pack over.
topic.payoff: Test: read the back first. If the front still feels true, buy it.
topic.behaviour: Brands lead with 'no maida', 'no added sugar', 'clean' claims while using other sweeteners or oils.
topic.mechanism: A health word on the front lifts the price more than the recipe changes.
topic.group: Young urban shoppers trying to eat better
topic.send_to: The friend whose 'healthy' snack drawer costs more than dinner
topic.why_now: Health-label snacks now take up whole shelves and apps.
real_details: A person bought a makhana pack from an office vending machine for Rs 30. They couldn't see the weight beforehand, and it turned out to be only 12g.
The same buyer said the protein claim on the front was hard to read, either 8% or S%. They called the pack a scam and told others to avoid it in vending machines.
One commenter said this is called slack fill. They said other countries regulate pack size so it isn't visually misleading, while Indian law doesn't say what proper packaging should look like.
Another commenter joked that 12g of snack at that protein level works out to about 960mg of protein.
One commenter said farmers get roughly Rs 200-250 per kg of makhana, so the farmer and the labourer wouldn't see even Rs 5 from a pack like this. Another suggested filing a consumer court complaint.

score.why: The 'no refined sugar' granola is wellness as marketing, and the read-the-back-first test is easy to reuse.
